title: Hurricane Maria
description:
Interview (B) with Maj. Gen. Thomas J. Sharpy, Deputy Commanding General for Lt. Gen. Buchanan, at Muniz Air National Guard Base, Puerto Rico, Oct. 12, 2017.
Hurricane Maria formed in the Atlantic Ocean and affected islands in the Caribbean Sea, including Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. U.S. Military assets supported FEMA as well as state and local authorities in rescue and relief efforts. (U.S. Air Force video by Senior Airman Tayor Harrison)
keywords: ANG, relief efforts, Puerto Rico Air National Guard, Hurricane Maria, NGB, Puerto Rico

transcript.text: I'm the Deputy Commanding General for Lieutenant General Buchanan and since I've arrived I've
primarily been focusing on setting up the strategic airlift bridge that's been necessary
to bring the equipment, the personnel and all the supplies here to the island of Puerto
Rico.
So the role of the Air Force obviously it's an island destination and due to the destruction
that this island suffered the airports and the seaports were closed.
So as soon as the winds were within limits the contingency response forces of the United
States Air Force came in and opened up the airfield in San Juan.
Once they opened the airfield they then opened up the cargo yard so that we could bring in
the much needed supplies forces into this airfield and then once we opened San Juan we then went
to Roosevelt Roads which is on the eastern side of the island and once we opened up that
airfield and cargo handling facility we then looked to the western side of the island and
Agua Día where we had to do the same thing and then the last airfield we opened was Ponce
which is in the southern central part of the island and then beyond the airfields we then
are also evaluating the seaports we know the one in San Juan is operating but we're trying
to get another one opened in Ponce so that we can bring in the large container vessels
that bring in the majority of supplies whether it be on a daily basis that the people of Puerto
Rico need and also to sustain a large military presence that's here.
Well obviously being an island destination everything you can't drive it in by a truck.
Everything has to be delivered by either air or by sea and initially the seaports were closed
and so therefore all of the cargo all the personnel and all the supplies had to be air
lifted in and we've flown almost 1400 sorties just in support of our fellow citizens here
in Puerto Rico.
It's been pretty awesome you know the Lieutenant General Birkanen brought his staff here from
Army North and they are fine oiled machine you know they were in Texas dealing with
Harvey and then they were in Florida dealing with Irma and then they came here to deal
with Maria and they have a lot of experience doing this.
The challenge for me was trying to integrate the strategic airlift because in those other
instances they had a lot of ground movement and a lot of forces that they had that were
quickly able to respond whereas here we had to fly everything in and so that strategic
airlift piece was that critical lifeline between our North and North Com and support of FEMA
that was run out of Florida by First Air Force and so I was there just to integrate and make
sure that we met the priorities of not only the governor, FEMA but also General Buchanan
in his role as the Joint Forces Land Component Commander.
I would say the biggest challenge has been we have a lot of great people trying to do a
lot of incredible things we all realize the magnitude of trying to provide relief and
those critical supplies and medical capabilities to our fellow citizens.
The challenge has been to integrate all of those efforts into a cohesive plan.
FEMA has a way of doing things, the Army has a way of doing things, the Air Force has a
way of doing things, North Com has a way of doing things and just trying to coordinate
all those great efforts into a synchronized plan has been a challenge but I will tell
you I think we've done exceptionally well and I think the results that I've seen at all
the places that I've gotten to visit we're getting the commodities to the logistical staging
areas and we're using the municipalities and the mayors to distribute those goods to
getting them to the people that are in need.
It's going well, could it be better, absolutely but every day I've seen an improvement in
the teamwork has just been incredible.
I think the biggest success has been that this is in my 30 years in the Air Force I've
never seen us provide this much weight of effort for humanitarian assistance as a release
effort whether it be an aircraft, whether it be in personnel or whether it be in the
amount of DOD effort that we've put behind this.
You know we've moved over 1300 sorties just for Maria alone here in Puerto Rico and over
2000 within the US Virgin Islands and the Puerto Rican area of responsibility in the last
40 days.
That's incredible.
I got to tell you everywhere I've been including today when I was in Roosevelt Roads I saw an
airman who was on the flight line.
He was tired, he was dirty, he was thirsty and he was drenched in sweat but you know what
I've never seen Morale hire.
You know why?
Because he was doing what he wanted to do and he was doing it for a cause that's bigger
than himself because he knows that at the end of the day his efforts enable the relief supplies
to get to those families, to get to those children and without everyone who's here we wouldn't
be able to do what we're doing because we're making a difference.
I've seen it in the field, I've seen it when I delivered cargo to the isolated communities
in the mountains yesterday and when I got to see the smiles on the face of the children
and get to see people getting food and water every airman and every soldier that's here
and first of all the people of Puerto Ricans, they are dedicated, they are resilient, they
are passionate and as they've told me this is a storm.
It's not going to get in the way of them being a proud people that they are.
Specifically we talk about the Air National Guard and the reserve members that are here
in Puerto Rico.
Not only did they serve our country but they're also victims in this as well and so they're
not only proud of their service but they're also struggling with the devastation that them
and their families have felt and I will tell you they're the first ones to raise their hands
because they want to support their families and their fellow members in Puerto Rico.
Now what I found even more inspiring to me was how many people who are from Puerto Rico
who serve in our Department of Defense around the nation and around the world who volunteered
to be some of the first ones here to be able to be the translators, to be able to be the
facilitators because they're going back to their neighborhoods.
I talked to a Warren officer yesterday who had the ability to go back to a neighborhood
and the people were looking at him kind of puzzled and then they told him his name they
all said you're the little guy that used to cause trouble in the neighborhood and they
broke down and let him go because it was his neighborhood, it was his family that he
was providing support to and I've never seen a soldier more proud of what he's doing because
he's helping a neighborhood we grow up.
We say that the great news about our garden reserve is you live locally, serve globally
well when you get to live locally and serve locally that is a huge success and the fact
that they're leading a lot of the efforts matters because they believe that it's their
neighborhood, it's their families that they're helping and we're here to help support them
as well.
It's pretty cool.
I just like to add that when I first got here and I got to see the devastation in my
heart sunk.
What I saw in the press before I left Scott Air Force Base and got an airplane to come
here I knew that it was bad but when I saw the devastation firsthand first by flying
around the country second by driving to some of the locations my heart sank and the good
news is the people are resilient.
I was blown away by how supportive they were, how happy they were and how they were really
ready to get on to get back to normal and get on with their lives.
Our goal is to get that to happen sooner rather than later and that's why we've had so many
incredible support from the Department of Defense and in fact when the President said you have
everything you need I looked him in the eye and said yes we do because we're not shying
away from this one and we're not going to leave until the normal is back here in Puerto
Rico.
